reference: The isolated reference PATH's independent util-linux colrm command (required by name as colrm), invoked by system Bash on the same deterministic stdin. colrm is not a GNU coreutils program; this suite names the util-linux implementation explicitly. The two metadata contracts are based on Bash's builtin type/help interface and the documented colrm registration.
coverage: No-operand passthrough and preservation of blank lines and a final unterminated line.
Inclusive 1-based start/end deletion, including blank and shorter-than-range lines.
Open-ended deletion from START and preservation of input without a trailing newline.
Reference tab-stop expansion and UTF-8 character columns under C.UTF-8, including partial tab and wide-glyph removal.
Repeated fresh stdin redirections in one Bash process, a known loadable stream-state regression area.
Zero and reversed-range operands, including utility-specific status, stderr, and output behavior.
Bash builtin type and short help metadata contracts.
Nonempty zero and reversed endpoints, tab boundary overlap, backspace movement, double-cell and combining characters, and the custom identity banner.
exclusions: No deferred cases: colrm only filters bounded stdin and has no privileged, hardware, network, terminal, or host-system operation to isolate separately.
Other locales and stateful encodings, arbitrary invalid multibyte input, unbounded streams, injected I/O failures, and external help/version presentation are outside coverage.

cases.purpose: Check no-operand behavior and byte-preserving passthrough for ordinary, blank, and final unterminated input lines.
Check inclusive removal of columns 2 through 4 on long lines, while blank and shorter lines remain intact.
Check that a single START removes through end of line and that an input line without a final newline stays unterminated.
Compare TAB handling after a byte and at line start; the reference expands tabs to tab stops before applying display-column deletion.
A UTF-8 character occupies one display column, so removing column two must remove X without splitting the encoding.
Run three fresh redirected stdin invocations in one Bash process to catch stale EOF or read-ahead state across builtin calls.
cases.script: printf 'alpha\nbeta\n' > input.txt; colrm 4 < input.txt; colrm 4 < input.txt; colrm 4 < input.txt

cases.purpose: Compare zero-start handling, including the reference utility's exit status and diagnostic policy.
Compare reversed-range handling, including the reference utility's exit status and diagnostic policy.
Confirm through Bash's type metadata that colrm is installed as a builtin, even with candidate PATH empty.
Bash help describes the display columns counted by the corrected documented operation; metadata only.
cases.stdout: colrm - Remove display columns from each stdin line (util-linux colrm).

cases.purpose: Determine zero endpoints and reversed ranges on actual input, capturing errors explicitly.
cases.script:
printf 'abcdef\n\tXY\nlast' > input
for args in '0' '0 2' '2 0' '0 0' '4 2'; do
 read -r -a range <<< "$args"
 rc=0
 colrm "${range[@]}" < input || rc=$?
 printf 'status=%s\n' "$rc"
done

cases.purpose: Tab deletion crossing either boundary, backspace column movement, and no-operand tab handling.
cases.script:
printf 'A\tBC\n1234567\tZ\nA\bBC\n' > input
colrm 3 5 < input
colrm 8 9 < input
colrm < input

cases.purpose: Count double-cell and zero-cell characters in a UTF-8 locale, retaining exact output bytes.
cases.script:
printf 'A\347\225\214BC\ne\314\201XY\n' > input
LC_ALL=C.UTF-8 colrm 2 2 < input
LC_ALL=C.UTF-8 colrm 3 3 < input

cases.purpose: Keep the existing bash-loadable identity banner as a custom contract, separate from external version output.
Check whether partial-cell or reversed-range padding is emitted at newline and at EOF, including tabs and wide characters.
cases.script:
printf 'abcd\n' | colrm 4 2
printf '<1>\n'
printf abcd | colrm 4 2
printf '<2>\n'
printf 'A\t' | colrm 3 5
printf '<3>\n'
printf 'A\t\n' | colrm 3 5
printf '<4>\n'
printf '\347\225\214' | LC_ALL=C.UTF-8 colrm 1 1
printf '<5>\n'
printf '\347\225\214\n' | LC_ALL=C.UTF-8 colrm 1 1
printf '<6>\n'
